svg.title: Molecular profile and the direction of adjuvant treatment: four classes, PORTEC-4a read out, four RAINBO arms ongoing
svg.desc: Schematic: where the molecular profile pushes adjuvant treatment, and why direction is not the same as strength. The upper block shows the four PORTEC-3 classes (10-year molecular analysis, 411 of 660 evaluable, high-risk population, FIGO 2009), the whole block labelled "all post-hoc analyses". POLE mutant (n=51): 10-year overall survival 98.0 per cent (94.3 to 100.0); chemoradiotherapy 100.0 against radiotherapy alone 96.4 per cent, compared by log-rank with p = 0.40 and no hazard ratio reported for this box; direction marked de-escalation, with the authors concluding that irrespective of stage, and on the basis of excellent recurrence-free survival, de-escalation should be recommended for POLE mutant cancers, preferably in a study setting. MMRd, mismatch repair deficient (n=139): 10-year overall survival 71.7 per cent (64.2 to 80.0); chemoradiotherapy 68.7 against radiotherapy alone 74.4 per cent, adjusted hazard ratio 1.34, 95 per cent confidence interval 0.71 to 2.55, p = 0.37, drawn as an interval crossing the dashed line at 1; this box is labelled "unfavourable direction, not significant, small n", with a note that none of the three labels may be dropped, so it can neither be read as chemotherapy helping here nor, in the other direction, as chemotherapy not being needed. NSMP, no specific molecular profile (n=122): 10-year overall survival 77.9 per cent (70.7 to 85.8); chemoradiotherapy 81.2 against radiotherapy alone 74.1 per cent, adjusted hazard ratio 0.60 (0.27 to 1.32), p = 0.21, the interval again crossing 1 and the box labelled not significant; the authors add that for oestrogen-receptor-positive tumours the benefit of chemotherapy may be smaller than hypothesised and hormonal therapy could be an alternative. p53 abnormal (n=99): 10-year overall survival 45.1 per cent (36.2 to 56.1); chemoradiotherapy 52.7 against radiotherapy alone 36.6 per cent, adjusted hazard ratio 0.52 (0.30 to 0.91), p = 0.021, the interval not crossing 1, direction marked escalation and the box carrying a "post-hoc analysis" tag; 10-year recurrence-free survival was 52.6 against 37.0 per cent, adjusted hazard ratio 0.42 (0.24 to 0.74), p = 0.0027. The middle block is PORTEC-4a, tagged "has read out" and "non-inferiority": n=564 evaluable (molecular profile group 367, standard group 197), early-stage high-intermediate risk, eight European countries, median age 69.0 years, median follow-up 58.1 months, randomised 2:1. The 367 women of the molecular profile group are drawn as a proportional bar in three parts: favourable 168 (46 per cent) observed with no adjuvant treatment at all; intermediate 148 (40 per cent) given vaginal brachytherapy, 21 Gy in 3 fractions; unfavourable 51 (14 per cent) given pelvic radiotherapy, 45.0 to 48.6 Gy. The primary endpoint, the 5-year cumulative incidence of vaginal recurrence, was 4.5 per cent (2.23 to 6.76) in the molecular profile group against 1.6 per cent (0.00 to 3.32) in the standard group, hazard ratio 2.71 (0.79 to 9.34); the upper bound of the one-sided confidence interval for the difference, 5.3 percentage points, lies below the pre-set non-inferiority margin of 7.0, p for non-inferiority = 0.005, drawn as a scale with the upper bound inside the margin and a note that non-inferiority proves the difference did not cross a line agreed in advance, not that the two are the same. In the favourable subgroup, the second primary analysis, 5-year vaginal recurrence was 4.1 per cent (0.81 to 7.37) against 0.9 per cent (0.00 to 2.78), hazard ratio 3.97 (0.48 to 32.95): the point estimate is fourfold, and it sits inside the margin only because the denominator is small and the interval so wide as to carry almost no information. A starred panel states that favourable is not the same as POLE mutant: in PORTEC-4a favourable means POLE mutant, or NSMP with wild-type CTNNB1, and the whole risk profile also takes in L1CAM overexpression and substantial lymphovascular space invasion, so reading it as "POLE mutation means no treatment" is wrong. Adverse events were mostly grade 1-2, with grade 3 or worse genitourinary toxicity in 4 of 367 (1 per cent) against 4 of 197 (2 per cent). The next block gives the four RAINBO colours, every row tagged "ongoing": p53abn-RED, for p53 abnormal, maintenance olaparib for 2 years after adjuvant chemoradiotherapy against chemoradiotherapy alone, planned 554, phase 3; MMRd-GREEN, radiotherapy with concurrent and adjuvant durvalumab for 1 year against radiotherapy alone, planned 316, phase 3; NSMP-ORANGE, for oestrogen-receptor-positive NSMP, a de-escalation of radiotherapy followed by 2 years of progestogen against chemoradiotherapy, planned 600, phase 3; and POLEmut-BLUE, a de-escalation with no adjuvant treatment, or none or radiotherapy alone for higher-risk patients, planned 145, phase 2. Beside them a timeline headed "timing: around 2030" gives December 2028 for the primary completion of RAINBO BLUE & TAPER (NCT05640999, 393 patients), January 2030 for the RAINBO umbrella trial (NCT05255653, estimated 1,615), and June 2030 for RAINBO-RED (NCT06712472, 554); a note records that the protocol paper expected main results from 2028 while the registry dates are later, so anyone deciding this year is still working from the post-hoc analyses above and one non-inferiority trial. At the foot of the figure a gold-bordered panel states that for most women with early-stage disease this does not change the treatment: in a prospective real-world study that put molecular classification into the multidisciplinary meeting, of 122 women after surgery with FIGO 2023 stage 1 to 2 disease the recommendation changed in only 25 (20.5 per cent), escalated in 15 (12.3 per cent) and de-escalated in 10 (8.2 per cent), the changes concentrated in the TP53-abnormal group (62.5 per cent against 10.2 per cent in the rest), with no NSMP or POLE mutant case changed - a single-institution study from India of 122 women covering only stage 1 to 2, so not strong evidence. The panel closes by saying that the figure shows direction rather than strength and that the strength of evidence differs from box to box - the PORTEC-3 molecular comparisons are post-hoc, PORTEC-4a proves non-inferiority, RAINBO has no results yet - and that whether anything is added or taken away is a conversation with the gynaecological oncology, radiation oncology and medical oncology teams. A further note records that fewer than 5 per cent have multiple classifiers, assigned in the order POLE mutant, then MMRd, then p53 abnormal.

g.text: MOLECULAR PROFILE AND THE DIRECTION OF ADJUVANT TREATMENT
Where the molecular profile pushes treatment - direction is not
The direction of each of the four types comes from the 10-year molecular analysis of PORTEC-3 (411 of 660 evaluable, high-risk
population, FIGO 2009). This is a post-hoc analysis: randomisation was not stratified by molecular class.
The two blocks below are kept apart: what has already read out (PORTEC-4a), and what is still recruiting (the four RAINBO arms).
The four PORTEC-3 classes: 10-year overall survival, and chemoradiotherapy against radiotherapy
Brackets give 95% confidence intervals. The dashed line is 1: an interval crossing it means this trial cannot show a direction.

A prospective real-world study put molecular classification into the multidisciplinary meeting: of 122 women after surgery with FIGO 2023 stage 1 to 2 disease,
the recommendation changed in only 25 (20.5 per cent) - escalated in 15 (12.3 per cent), de-escalated in 10 (8.2 per cent); the changes were concentrated in the
TP53-abnormal group (62.5 per cent, against 10.2 per cent in the rest), and no NSMP or POLE mutant case had its treatment changed. This is a single-institution
study from India of 122 women covering only stage 1 to 2; the evidence is not strong, so remember the direction rather than the number.
Fewer than 5 per cent have multiple classifiers; they are assigned in the order POLE mutant, then MMRd, then p53 abnormal.

Schematic, redrawn from the PORTEC-3 10-year results and post-hoc molecular analysis (Post 2025), PORTEC-4a (van den Heerik 2026), the RAINBO protocol paper (2023) and
the ClinicalTrials.gov records (NCT05255653, NCT06712472, NCT05640999, consulted 10 September 2026), the ESGO-ESTRO-ESP 2025 update, and a prospective real-world
study (Pinninti 2026); the cohorts, designs and endpoints of the underlying studies differ, so the data points must not be compared directly.
